vectors.title: unreserved characters are decoded before dot-segments are resolved
vectors.why: The order is the whole check. `.` is unreserved, so %2E%2E decodes to a real `..` and — followed by a literal slash — becomes a segment that must be resolved away. An implementation that resolves before decoding leaves the escape intact through normalization, where it re-expands downstream after the verifier has approved it.

vectors.title: a reserved character stays encoded, so %2F never becomes a path separator
vectors.why: The other half of the same rule, and the one that looks like a bug until you see it. Only *unreserved* characters are decoded — `/` is a reserved delimiter, so %2E%2E%2F canonicalizes to `..%2F`, a single opaque segment rather than a traversal. Decoding it would manufacture a path separator the requester never sent, which is a way to escape a grant rather than a way to enforce one.

vectors.title: a scheme default port is removed so one grant has one spelling
vectors.why: Otherwise https://h:443/x and https://h/x are two different grants for one resource.

vectors.title: userinfo in the authority is refused outright
vectors.why: https://evil.com@good.com/ is a read-the-wrong-host confusion with no legitimate use in a resource grant. Refusing is safer than picking a host.

vectors.title: a host wildcard matches exactly one non-empty label
vectors.why: *.example.com must not cover a.b.example.com. An implementation using a suffix match grants a whole subtree it was never given.

vectors.title: a narrower path prefix is contained by a wider one
vectors.why: The ordinary positive case, so a conforming implementation is not merely refusing everything.

vectors.title: each child pattern must be covered by one single parent pattern
vectors.why: Sound but incomplete on purpose: a child covered only by the union of two parent patterns is refused. Incompleteness costs an issuer an awkward error; unsoundness costs the principal their balance.
